1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: A 36-year-old man, Mr. Xu, from Gushi County, Henan Province, presented to our hospital on Day 0, with the chief complaint of intermittent cough, sputum production, chest pain, and fever for more than 1 year. One year before presentation, the patient developed cough, sputum production, and chest pain without an obvious precipitating cause. The chest pain was mainly dull pain, worsened after activity, and was accompanied by fever, with a maximum temperature of 38.4℃. There was no wheezing or chest tightness. Chest CT performed at a local county hospital showed inflammation in the right upper lobe, and follow-up reexamination after treatment was recommended. After half a month of anti-infective and symptomatic treatment, the symptoms improved, but repeat chest CT showed no obvious absorption. Subsequently, the patient presented to a hospital in Anhui Province, where bronchoscopy showed a polypoid neoplasm protruding into the lumen in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe, with complete obstruction of the lumen. Pathologic biopsy findings were consistent with inflammatory changes, with no definite evidence of malignancy. The patient was discharged after anti-infective treatment with symptomatic improvement. Thereafter, the above symptoms recurred repeatedly, and symptomatic treatment at the local hospital relieved the symptoms. The patient had previously been in good health, with no history of hypertension or heart disease, no history of diabetes or cerebrovascular disease, no history of hepatitis, TB, or malaria, and vaccination history according to the routine immunization program. There was no history of surgery, trauma, or blood transfusion, and no history of food or drug allergy. He had long resided locally in his hometown, with no history of exposure to epidemic areas, outbreaks, or contaminated water; no history of residence in pastoral areas, mining areas, high-fluoride areas, or low-iodine areas; no history of exposure to chemical substances, radioactive substances, or toxic substances; no history of drug abuse; no history of smoking or alcohol use; and denied a history of commercial sexual activity. Marital and reproductive history: married, married at age 30, spouse healthy, harmonious marital relationship, with 3 sons. Family history: parents healthy, siblings healthy, no similar disease in the family, and no family history of hereditary disease. Physical examination after admission showed: temperature 36.5℃, pulse 92/min, respirations 18/min, blood pressure 120/80mmHg. Respiratory movement was normal, intercostal spaces were normal, tactile fremitus was normal, no pleural friction fremitus, no subcutaneous crepitus, percussion was resonant, breath sounds were clear in both lungs, with no dry or wet rales, no pleural friction rub, and normal vocal resonance. Relevant examinations were completed on Day 0: CBC, blood biochemistry, and coagulation tests showed no obvious abnormalities; ESR (laser method) 1.00mm/h, CRP 1.05 mg/L, PCT <0.020ng/mL, T-SPOT well A 24, well B 21, and tumor markers were normal. ECG showed ST-T changes in the inferior leads. Chest CT showed inflammation in the right upper lobe. Bronchoscopy was performed, and a soft tissue shadow obstructing the lumen was seen in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe; biopsy of the right upper lobe bronchus was performed, and pathologic biopsy returned as chronic mucosal inflammation with focal squamous metaplasia of the epithelium and granulation tissue hyperplasia. After discharge, the patient continued to have intermittent chest pain and fever as described above, and returned to our outpatient clinic for repeat chest CT, which showed little change compared with the prior film of Day 0; he was not hospitalized for treatment. One year ago, the patient again developed the above symptoms of cough, sputum production, chest pain, and fever, and presented to the Department of Thoracic Surgery at our hospital. Chest CT showed right upper lobe inflammation, slightly worse than before. Outside the hospital, the patient continued to have recurrent chest pain and fever as described above, and presented again to our department on Day +1104.

differential_diagnoses.name: Central bronchogenic carcinoma (possible squamous cell carcinoma)
supporting_evidence: Symptoms persisted and recurred for more than 1 year, manifested as intermittent cough, sputum production, chest pain, and fever. After anti-infective treatment, only the symptoms improved, but there was no significant absorption on chest CT.

Repeated chest CT scans showed inflammation in the right upper lobe, with little change on follow-up compared with prior imaging and slight subsequent worsening compared with earlier studies, consistent with the imaging features of recurrent post-obstructive infection/atelectasis.

Bronchoscopy showed a polypoid neoplasm protruding into the lumen of the anterior segment of the right upper lobe, with complete obstruction of the lumen; on this bronchoscopy, a soft tissue opacity was also seen obstructing the lumen of the anterior segment of the right upper lobe, suggesting a persistent endobronchial space-occupying lesion.

Pathology showed only chronic mucosal inflammation with focal squamous metaplasia of the epithelium and granulation tissue proliferation; this was a small biopsy specimen, and missed diagnosis of a tumor due to insufficient sampling cannot be completely excluded.
The attached images show a localized abnormal opacity in the right upper lung and a polypoid endobronchial lesion on bronchoscopy, supporting the presence of an obstructive endobronchial lesion
opposing_evidence: The patient is 36 years old and has no smoking history.
Neither of the two previous bronchoscopic biopsies showed definite evidence of malignancy.
Tumor markers were normal
Routine blood test, CRP, PCT, and ESR showed no obvious abnormalities, lacking clear evidence of tumor-related systemic inflammation or progression.

differential_diagnoses.name: Endobronchial TB/tuberculous bronchial stenosis with obstructive pneumonia
supporting_evidence: The course has been prolonged and recurrent, mainly involving the right upper lobe, with long-term recurrent cough, sputum production, and fever, consistent with the characteristic chronic recurrent presentation of TB or endobronchial TB.
T-SPOT: well A 24, well B 21, indicating a positive immunologic test for TB infection

Bronchoscopy showed a polypoid neoplasm in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe, completely obstructing the lumen; endobronchial TB can form granulation tissue, scarring, or intraluminal proliferative changes.
Biopsy pathology showed chronic inflammation with granulation tissue proliferation, which may partially overlap with the features of tuberculous inflammation
The attached image shows a persistent fixed lesion in the right upper lung, consistent with secondary changes following localized bronchial obstruction.
opposing_evidence: No definite history of TB in the past medical history
Pathology did not suggest more specific evidence of TB, such as caseous necrosis or tuberculous granulomas.
ESR 1.00 mm/h, CRP 1.05 mg/L, PCT <0.020 ng/mL; markers of active inflammation are not elevated
The first-stage information did not provide positive evidence of sputum acid-fast bacilli, Mycobacterium tuberculosis nucleic acid, or culture.

differential_diagnoses.name: Bronchial carcinoid (central neuroendocrine tumor)
supporting_evidence: The patient is relatively young, 36 years old; central carcinoid can be seen in younger patients.

Bronchoscopy showed a polypoid neoplasm protruding into the lumen and completely obstructing the anterior segmental bronchus of the right upper lobe, consistent with the common endobronchial growth pattern of carcinoid.
Recurrent inflammatory opacity fixed in the right upper lobe, suggesting postobstructive infection caused by a central airway mass
Prior and current small biopsy specimens showed only inflammatory changes; a central carcinoid may not be definitively diagnosed because of limited sampling.
Normal tumor markers cannot exclude bronchial carcinoid.
opposing_evidence: The phase I information did not describe accompanying manifestations such as hemoptysis, flushing, and diarrhea that may suggest carcinoid.
Pathology showed no definite evidence of neuroendocrine tumor
Phase 1 information did not provide obvious hypervascular features on contrast-enhanced CT or bronchoscopy.

differential_diagnoses.name: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor/inflammatory pseudotumor or bronchial inflammatory polyp
supporting_evidence: Pathologic biopsy showed chronic mucosal inflammation with focal squamous metaplasia of the epithelium and granulation tissue proliferation, supporting an inflammatory or reactive lesion.
Bronchoscopy showed a polypoid lesion obstructing the lumen; inflammatory polyps or inflammatory pseudotumors may present as polypoid endobronchial masses.
Symptoms can be relieved after anti-infective and symptomatic treatment, suggesting the presence of an inflammatory component
The patient is young, has no smoking history, and does not have prominent traditional risk factors for malignant tumors.
opposing_evidence: The lesions have persisted for many years, and on follow-up chest CT there has been little change or even slight worsening; a purely inflammatory lesion would typically show more obvious resolution or fluctuation.
Complete bronchial lumen obstruction that is persistent over a long period requires a high degree of suspicion for a neoplastic lesion rather than simple inflammation.
The phase I information did not provide more specific pathological evidence for inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.

differential_diagnoses.name: Benign endobronchial tumors (such as squamous cell papilloma, hamartoma, adenoma, etc.)
supporting_evidence: Bronchoscopy repeatedly showed a soft tissue/polypoid lesion in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe protruding into the lumen and causing complete obstruction, consistent with localized obstruction caused by a benign endobronchial tumor.
Pathology showed no definite evidence of malignant tumor.
The localized lesion has been present for a long time and has changed slowly, which is consistent with the slow-growth characteristics of some benign tumors.
The attached image shows a focal right upper lobe lesion rather than diffuse disease, supporting a localized endobronchial etiology.
opposing_evidence: Biopsy pathology mainly showed chronic inflammation and granulation tissue proliferation, and did not directly support any specific type of benign biliary tumor.
The presence of fever and recurrent inflammation more often suggests post-obstructive infection and cannot explain the nature of the primary lesion.
The phase I information did not provide typical imaging features, such as fat or popcorn calcification of a hamartoma.

differential_diagnoses.name: Retained bronchial foreign body with granulation tissue proliferation and recurrent obstructive infection
supporting_evidence: The lesion is confined to the right upper lobe and has recurred repeatedly. Bronchoscopy showed complete obstruction of the lumen, and biopsy demonstrated granulation tissue proliferation, consistent with the possibility of a granulation reaction following foreign body irritation.
Symptoms may improve after anti-infective treatment, but the imaging findings do not resolve, suggesting the presence of a persistent mechanical obstructive factor.
The attached image shows a localized fixed pulmonary opacity, supporting post-obstructive changes secondary to localized airway obstruction.
opposing_evidence: The phase 1 information did not provide a definite history of choking, aspiration, or foreign body inhalation.
Bronchoscopy described a polypoid lesion/soft tissue lesion; no foreign body was directly visualized.
The clinical course was very long, but no evidence of a foreign body was documented on multiple examinations.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Fiberoptic bronchoscopy was performed. Bronchoscopy showed a neoplasm within the lumen of the anterior segmental bronchus of the right upper lobe, completely obstructing the lumen; the bronchial mucosa in the remaining bronchi of both lungs was smooth, and the lumens were patent.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had recurrent cough, sputum production, chest pain, and fever for 4 years. After anti-infective treatment, the symptoms were only temporarily relieved, but the right upper lobe lesion remained persistently nonresolving and gradually worsened. Chest CT indicated stenosis and occlusion of the right upper lobe bronchus and typical obstructive pneumonia, indicating the need for direct evaluation of whether there is persistent mechanical obstruction within the airway. Although bronchoscopy had been performed previously, the lesion has persisted and imaging has progressed, so repeat fiberoptic bronchoscopy is needed for direct visualization of the lesion location, extent, degree of obstruction, and the condition of the remaining bronchi, in order to determine whether it is a central tumor, inflammatory polyp, tuberculous bronchial lesion, or other benign endobronchial tumor, and to provide a basis for subsequent biopsy sampling and treatment selection. This examination can also determine whether the lesion completely obstructs the bronchial lumen and its impact on ventilation and drainage, and assess the need for continued endoscopic management versus referral for surgical treatment.

recommended_exams.exam: Bronchial biopsy of the anterior segment of the right upper lobe
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Bronchial biopsy of the anterior segment of the right upper lobe
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Bronchoscopy has already revealed a neoplasm in the anterior segmental bronchus of the right upper lobe completely obstructing the lumen, while the patient has had a protracted course with recurrent post-obstructive infection. Multiple prior small biopsies showed only inflammatory changes, which cannot explain the intraluminal space-occupying lesion that has persisted for years and progressed, raising the possibility of insufficient sampling or failure to obtain the lesional tissue itself. Therefore, the definite obstructive lesion must be biopsied again to obtain histopathologic evidence and distinguish among malignant tumor, bronchial carcinoid, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, hamartoma, neurogenic or other mesenchymal lesions, as well as endobronchial TB-related granulomatous tissue proliferation. This examination is directly related to establishing the definitive nature of the lesion, determining whether surgical resection is needed, and avoiding long-term treatment of a potentially resectable tumor as simple infection.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Pathology showed chronic mucosal inflammation, with proliferating spindle cells seen in the submucosa
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Pathologic examination must be performed after biopsy because the patient’s core clinical problem is a long-standing fixed endobronchial occupying lesion causing recurrent obstructive pneumonia, and the nature of the lesion cannot be determined by symptoms, CT, and bronchoscopic morphology alone. Pathologic examination can first differentiate, at the level of tissue architecture, simple chronic inflammation, granulation tissue, epithelial neoplasms, mesenchymal tumors, or other rare benign or malignant lesions. In this case, pathology showed submucosal proliferation of spindle cells, suggesting that the lesion was not a simple infection and further advancing the diagnosis from “inflammation of unclear nature” toward a “spindle cell lesion,” providing key clues for subsequent immunohistochemistry and surgical decision-making, and also helping explain why the imaging findings did not resolve for a long time after anti-infective treatment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Immunohistochemistry: AE1/AE3 (-), S-100 (+), SOX-10 (-), SMA (occasional+), Desmin (occasional+), Ki-67 (3%+)
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: When pathology shows only spindle cell proliferation, immunohistochemistry is a key adjunct for clarifying the direction of tumor differentiation and the tendency toward benignity or malignancy. The patient is young and has no smoking history, but has a persistent endoluminal obstructive lesion and recurrent infection; previous small biopsies were all inconclusive, so immunophenotyping is required to differentiate epithelial malignant tumors, neuroendocrine tumors, smooth muscle or myogenic lesions, nerve sheath-related lesions, and mesenchymal or mixed lesions such as hamartoma. Negative AE1/AE3 helps reduce the likelihood of epithelial carcinoma, and positive S-100 combined with a low Ki-67 supports a benign mesenchymal/hamartomatous direction, which can reduce the risk of misdiagnosing a malignant tumor and guide whether surgical resection should be the main treatment and prognosis assessment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Intraoperative rapid frozen-section pathology was consistent with chondromatous hamartoma, with myxoid degeneration
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Because of long-term endobronchial obstruction, progressively worsening imaging findings, and the eventual development of typical obstructive pneumonia, the patient ultimately required surgical management; however, the preoperative biopsy still could not completely exclude malignancy or other lesions requiring more extensive resection. The purpose of intraoperative rapid frozen-section pathology is to confirm the nature of the lesion as quickly as possible during surgery and to answer key questions such as whether this is a benign hamartoma or a malignant tumor, and whether the extent of resection is adequate. If the frozen section supports a benign hamartoma, unnecessarily extensive resection can be avoided; if it suggests malignancy, the surgical plan must be adjusted promptly to ensure surgical margins and curative resection. Therefore, this examination plays a direct role in establishing the diagnosis, assessing surgical strategy, and reducing the risk of overtreatment or undertreatment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Postoperative final pathology showed: hamartoma with organizing pneumonia changes in the surrounding lung tissue; nodular granulomatous inflammation with necrosis was also seen.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although frozen section pathology can provide intraoperative guidance, the final definitive diagnosis still depends on comprehensive sampling and systematic evaluation of the complete specimen on postoperative final surgical pathology. The patient had long-term recurrent inflammation in the right upper lobe and complete bronchial obstruction; in addition to confirming the nature of the endobronchial tumor itself, it was also necessary to explain the cause of the persistent nonresolving changes and progressive consolidation in the surrounding lung tissue. Postoperative final surgical pathology not only ultimately confirmed hamartoma, but also revealed surrounding organizing pneumonia changes, indicating that the recurrent symptoms were related to secondary changes after long-term obstruction; it also found nodular granulomatous inflammation with necrosis, suggesting that in addition to hamartoma there was also an infectious lesion requiring further investigation, especially clues to tuberculous disease. This examination is therefore crucial to the complete diagnostic assessment, postoperative follow-up testing, and decisions regarding anti-infective/anti-tuberculosis treatment.

After the postoperative final pathology revealed necrotizing nodular granulomatous inflammation, pathologic evaluation for Mycobacterium tuberculosis must be performed. The patient had a prior history of long-term cough, sputum production, and fever; the lesion was located in the right upper lobe and the disease course was prolonged. There had also been an earlier positive T-SPOT clue, so clinically differentiation from endobronchial TB or pulmonary TB was already necessary. Acid-fast staining can directly detect acid-fast bacilli and is a routine and important test in necrotizing granulomatous lesions, helping determine whether active TB infection is present. Although the result was negative in this case, a negative result cannot completely exclude TB, especially when the bacillary burden is low or sampling is limited. Therefore, its value also lies in indicating that molecular testing should be combined for further confirmation, to avoid missing a TB diagnosis based only on morphology or a single negative result.

Although postoperative permanent pathology had already identified necrotizing nodular granuloma and the pathologic acid-fast stain was negative, it remained a critical clinical question to determine whether TB was also present. The patient had long-term recurrent fever, cough, and sputum production; a persistent right upper lobe lesion; and histologic necrotizing granuloma, all of which made TB a coexisting diagnosis that had to be confirmed. TB-DNA testing can improve the detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis when acid-fast staining is negative, helping differentiate nonspecific granuloma from tuberculous lesions. In this case, the positive TB-DNA result ultimately provided the missing etiologic evidence, indicating that the patient did not simply have a purely endobronchial hamartoma, but rather hamartoma with coexisting TB, which was निर्णsive for the final diagnosis, whether to initiate postoperative anti-TB treatment, explaining the recurrent inflammatory manifestations, and subsequent follow-up management.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Fiberoptic bronchoscopy was completed. Bronchoscopy showed a neoplasm completely obstructing the lumen of the anterior segmental bronchus of the right upper lobe; the bronchial mucosa of the remaining bronchi in both lungs was smooth, and the lumens were patent. A biopsy was performed at the anterior segmental bronchus of the right upper lobe. Pathology reported chronic inflammation of the mucosa, with proliferating spindle cells seen in the submucosa. Immunohistochemistry: AE1/AE3(-), S-100(+), SOX-10(-), SMA(focally+), Desmin(focally+), Ki-67(3%+). Intraoperatively, a gray-yellow nodule measuring approximately 1.5×0.8×0.7 was seen within the lumen of the right upper lobe bronchus; the cut surface of the nodule was gray-yellow, soft in texture, and relatively well demarcated. In addition, approximately 4 cm from the bronchial resection margin and approximately 0.5 cm from the pleura, a firm nodule about 0.4 cm in diameter was palpated; the cut surface of the nodule was gray-brown, medium in texture, and relatively well demarcated. Intraoperative rapid frozen-section pathology was consistent with chondromatous hamartoma with myxoid degeneration. Final postoperative pathology reported: hamartoma with organizing pneumonia changes in the surrounding lung tissue; in addition, nodular granulomatous inflammation with necrosis was seen. Pathologic acid-fast stain was negative, and TB-DNA was positive.
